title: Predict the output: a parent-type reference pointing to a child object calling a static method with the same signature — why does it print the parent's version (static method hiding, compile-time binding)?
shortTitle: Predict the output: parent reference calling static method

s1_definition.profdef: When a subclass declares a static method with the same signature as a static method in its superclass, the subclass method does not override the superclass method; it hides it. Static methods are resolved by static binding at compile time based on the declared type of the reference, not by dynamic dispatch at runtime based on the object's actual class. Therefore a reference of the parent type pointing at a child object invokes the parent's static method, because the compiler bound the call to the declared parent type. This is method hiding, and it is fundamentally different from instance-method overriding, which uses dynamic binding.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the method is a rulebook printed on the counter sign at National Bank of India. A static method is a rule written on the sign of the counter you walked up to, decided by which sign you are standing in front of, which is the declared type. An instance method is a rule the actual teller follows, decided by who the teller really is, which is the runtime object. If you stand at the counter labelled "Savings" but the person behind it happens to also be trained for "Current", the static sign still says "Savings rules" because the sign is chosen by where you stand, not by who the teller really is. So a parent-labelled counter prints the parent's rule even if a child is behind it.
s1_definition.oneliner: Static methods are hidden, not overridden, and are bound at compile time to the reference's declared type, so a parent reference calls the parent's static method regardless of the actual object.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** When a subclass declares a static method with the same signature as a static method in its superclass, the subclass method does not override the superclass method; it hides it. Static methods are resolved by static binding at compile time based on the declared type of the reference, not by dynamic dispatch at runtime based on the object's actual class. Therefore a reference of the parent type pointing at a child object invokes the parent's static method, because the compiler bound the call to the declared parent type. This is method hiding, and it is fundamentally different from instance-method overriding, which uses dynamic binding.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the method is a rulebook printed on the counter sign at National Bank of India. A static method is a rule written on the sign of the counter you walked up to, decided by which sign you are standing in front of, which is the declared type. An instance method is a rule the actual teller follows, decided by who the teller really is, which is the runtime object. If you stand at the counter labelled "Savings" but the person behind it happens to also be trained for "Current", the static sign still says "Savings rules" because the sign is chosen by where you stand, not by who the teller really is. So a parent-labelled counter prints the parent's rule even if a child is behind it.

**One line to remember:** Static methods are hidden, not overridden, and are bound at compile time to the reference's declared type, so a parent reference calls the parent's static method regardless of the actual object.

sections.s2_technical:
Java has two completely different mechanisms for choosing which method body runs. Instance methods use dynamic dispatch, also called late binding or runtime polymorphism. The JVM looks at the actual runtime class of the object and calls that class's version, which is why overriding works and why a parent reference to a child object calls the child's overridden instance method. Static methods use static binding, also called early binding, where the compiler decides which method to call based purely on the compile-time type of the reference, and this decision is burned into the bytecode and never revisited at runtime.

When a subclass defines a static method with the same name and parameter list as a static method in the superclass, the language does not treat this as overriding, because overriding is defined only for instance methods that participate in dynamic dispatch. Instead the subclass's static method hides the superclass's static method. Both methods exist; which one you reach depends entirely on how you refer to it. If you call it through the child type or class name, you get the child's version; if you call it through the parent type or class name, you get the parent's version.

The surprising case is calling a static method through an object reference, which the language permits but discourages. Even though you write `ref.staticMethod()`, the compiler ignores the runtime object entirely and uses the declared type of `ref` to pick the method. So if `ref` is declared as the parent type but holds a child object, the compiler binds to the parent's static method, and that is what prints. This is why most style guides and compilers warn you to call static methods through the class name, like `Parent.staticMethod()`, because calling them through an instance reference is misleading: it looks like dynamic dispatch but is not.

A clarifying rule is that you cannot even use the usual override checks here. The `@Override` annotation on a hiding static method is a compile error, because the compiler knows static methods are not overridden. This is a useful diagnostic: if you intend to override and the compiler rejects your annotation, you have accidentally made the method static or changed the signature.

Contrast this with instance methods to cement the point. If both classes declared the same method as an instance method, a parent reference to a child object would call the child's version due to dynamic dispatch. Change only the keyword to static, and suddenly the parent reference calls the parent's version due to static binding. The single keyword flips the binding mechanism. The senior nuance is that fields behave like static methods in this respect: field access is also resolved by the declared type, not the runtime type, so a parent reference reads the parent's field even if the child shadows it. Only instance methods are dynamically dispatched. In banking code this matters when a utility base class and a specialized subclass both expose a static helper such as a fee calculator, and the result silently depends on the declared reference type rather than the real object, which is a subtle correctness trap.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India has a base AccountProcessor with a static method describing its processing tier, and a specialized SavingsProcessor that declares a static method with the identical signature intending to "override" the tier description. A developer holds a SavingsProcessor through an AccountProcessor-typed variable and calls the static method, expecting the savings description, but gets the base description. This is exactly how static method hiding works: the call is bound at compile time to the declared base type, so the base version runs.

Problem 2 — The team must understand why switching the very same method from static to instance changes the answer, so they can decide which they actually want. This is exactly the difference between static binding and dynamic dispatch: the instance version would print the subclass description, the static version prints the base description.

We will build a runnable demo with AccountProcessor and SavingsProcessor, each declaring both a static tier method and an instance tier method with the same signature. The demo holds a SavingsProcessor through an AccountProcessor reference and calls both, printing the static result bound to the declared type and the instance result dispatched to the runtime object, making the contrast explicit. The code includes the two classes and a demo main.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: an AccountProcessor-typed reference holding a SavingsProcessor object.

Step 1: At compile time the compiler sees the static call `ref.tierStatic()`. It looks at the declared type of `ref`, which is AccountProcessor, and binds the call to AccountProcessor's static method. This decision is written into the bytecode permanently.

Step 2: At runtime the JVM executes that pre-bound call. It does not consult the actual object at all for the static method, so it runs AccountProcessor's version and the result is the base tier description.

Step 3: The compiler then sees the instance call `ref.tierInstance()`. For instance methods it emits a virtual call that will be resolved at runtime against the actual object.

Step 4: At runtime the JVM looks at the real object, which is a SavingsProcessor, and dispatches to SavingsProcessor's overriding instance method, so the result is the savings tier description.

Step 5: The demo then calls the static method through each class name explicitly. AccountProcessor.tierStatic reaches the base version and SavingsProcessor.tierStatic reaches the child version, proving both static methods exist and are selected purely by the name or declared type used.

Step 6: The contrast is now explicit: with the same reference and the same object, the static call printed base and the instance call printed savings, demonstrating that the static keyword flips the binding from runtime dispatch to compile-time binding.

```
2026-10-30 17:56:40 INFO    Static via parent ref  -> BASE tier (static — bound to declared type)
2026-10-30 17:56:40 INFO    Instance via parent ref-> SAVINGS tier (instance — override wins via dynamic dispatch)
2026-10-30 17:56:40 INFO    AccountProcessor.tierStatic() -> BASE tier (static — bound to declared type)
2026-10-30 17:56:40 INFO    SavingsProcessor.tierStatic() -> SAVINGS tier (static — hides base, reached only via Savings type)
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```text
  AccountProcessor ref = new SavingsProcessor();
    │ declared type = AccountProcessor
    │ runtime object = SavingsProcessor
    │
    ├─ ref.tierStatic()  (STATIC → compile-time binding)
    │     compiler uses DECLARED type → AccountProcessor.tierStatic()
    │     ▼
    │   prints "BASE tier"   ← object IGNORED
    │
    └─ ref.tierInstance() (INSTANCE → dynamic dispatch)
          JVM uses RUNTIME object → SavingsProcessor.tierInstance()
          ▼
        prints "SAVINGS tier"  ← object CONSULTED

  Same reference, same object, opposite results — the 'static' keyword decides.
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Hiding vs Overriding ═══

  ┌─ Concept Map ──────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ static method + same signature → HIDING (early binding) │
  │ instance method + same signature → OVERRIDING (late)    │
  │ field + same name → SHADOWING (by declared type)        │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID / Rules ────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │ L: overriding preserves Liskov; hiding does NOT dispatch│
  │ Rule: call static via ClassName, never via instance ref │
  └────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ────────────────────────────────────────
  ┌────────────────────────────┐
  │ AccountProcessor           │
  │ + static tierStatic()      │  ← hidden by child
  │ + tierInstance()           │  ← overridden by child
  └─────────────┬──────────────┘
                │ extends
                ▼
  ┌────────────────────────────┐
  │ SavingsProcessor           │
  │ + static tierStatic()      │  HIDES (no @Override allowed)
  │ + @Override tierInstance() │  OVERRIDES
  └────────────────────────────┘

  ── Binding resolution table (in words) ──────────────────
  ref.tierStatic()   → declared type AccountProcessor → BASE
  ref.tierInstance() → runtime object SavingsProcessor → SAVINGS
  Savings.tierStatic()→ child static → SAVINGS

  Contract:
    Pre:  two static methods with same signature across parent/child
    Post: call resolves by DECLARED type, object ignored
    Diagnostic: @Override on static method = compile error
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
The output prints the parent's version, and the reason is that static methods are hidden, not overridden, and are resolved by static binding at compile time. Java has two distinct mechanisms for choosing a method body. Instance methods use dynamic dispatch, where the JVM looks at the actual runtime class of the object, which is why overriding works and a parent reference to a child object calls the child's instance method. Static methods use static binding, where the compiler decides which method to call based purely on the declared compile-time type of the reference, and that decision is baked into the bytecode and never reconsidered at runtime.

So when a subclass declares a static method with the same signature as the superclass, it does not override it, because overriding is defined only for instance methods that participate in dynamic dispatch. It hides it. Both methods exist, and which one you reach depends entirely on how you refer to it. Through the child type you get the child's version; through the parent type you get the parent's version. The surprising case is calling a static method through an object reference, which the language allows but discourages, because the compiler ignores the runtime object completely and uses the declared type of the reference. A parent-typed reference holding a child object therefore binds to and prints the parent's static method.

In a project at National Bank of India this exact trap appeared with an AccountProcessor base class and a SavingsProcessor subclass that both exposed a static tier-description helper. A developer held a SavingsProcessor through an AccountProcessor variable and called the static helper expecting the savings description, but got the base description, because the call was bound at compile time to the declared base type. The moment we changed that same method from static to an instance method, the answer flipped to the savings description, because instance methods dispatch on the real object. That single keyword changed the binding mechanism entirely, which is the crux of the question.

The rules I always state are these. Static methods and fields are resolved by the declared type of the reference, not the runtime type, so a parent reference reaches the parent's static method and the parent's field even when the child hides or shadows them. Only instance methods are dynamically dispatched to the real object. You should always call static methods through the class name rather than through an instance, precisely because calling them through an instance looks like dynamic dispatch but is not and misleads the reader. And a reliable diagnostic is that the override annotation on a hiding static method is a compile error, which tells you immediately that you have accidentally created a hidden static method instead of an overridden instance method.

---

keyPoints: Static methods are resolved by REFERENCE type, not object type
Parent p = new Child(); p.staticMethod() calls Parent.staticMethod()
This is method HIDING, not overriding — no polymorphism for static
Instance methods: runtime dispatch. Static methods: compile-time dispatch
